title: Global Skills Panel to Boost Incomes and Reduce Poverty
gist: The Center for Global Development and the World Bank Group are launching the Global Advisory Panel on Skills, a two-year systematic review intended to produce a "Smart Buys"-style list of the highest-return skills interventions in low- and middle-income countries. The stated problem is that registered studies on skills and job matching in LMICs have grown from almost none in 2013 to nearly 800 today while findings remain mixed on both effectiveness and return on investment, just as 1.2 billion young people are about to enter the labor force.

themes.theme: The scale of the skills problem

insights.claim: Over the next decade 1.2 billion young people will enter the labor force, most of them without strong foundational skills, credentials, or support to help them succeed.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Frames the size of the coming labor-supply shock in emerging economies, which determines whether the demographic dividend becomes growth or unemployment.
insights.locator: What is the Global Advisory Panel on Skills (GAPS) trying to answer?

insights.claim: The binding constraint is not only skills but the enabling environment, since many people in low- and middle-income countries lack the right skills for today's jobs and too few have the conditions to put those skills to use.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Implies training programs alone will underperform without complementary labor market and business-environment reforms, a common reason skills spending disappoints.
insights.locator: Many people in low- and middle-income countries

insights.claim: The skills mismatch manifests in three simultaneous failures: millions of workers without the skills employers need, skilled workers not linked to relevant job opportunities, and jobs that go unfilled.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a training problem from a matching problem, which determines whether the fix is education spending or job-matching infrastructure.

insights.claim: Poverty reduction has stagnated over the past decade despite a promising long arc of progress, while climate change and rapid advances in digital technology and AI are expected to widen the skills gap as they transform future jobs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: AI-driven task change is being treated by development institutions as a near-term poverty risk, which will pull donor funding toward reskilling programs.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, poverty reduction, despite a promising long arc

insights.claim: Registered studies with the American Economic Association registry on skills interventions and job matching for income generation in low- and middle-income countries have gone from almost none in 2013 to almost 800 today.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A hundredfold rise in registered trials means the constraint has shifted from generating evidence to synthesizing it, favoring institutions that own the synthesis layer.
insights.locator: The good news is the boom in evidence

insights.claim: More research has not produced more clarity: findings on skills interventions remain mixed both on whether they work and on what return they provide on investment.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: An honest admission from the institutions funding these programs that the ROI case for skills spending is currently unresolved, which should temper confidence in vocational-training investment theses.
insights.quote: But more research doesn't automatically mean more clarity.
insights.locator: But more research doesn't automatically mean more clarity

insights.claim: The chart documenting the surge in registered skills studies was produced as a Claude-generated graph from the AEA registry using keywords related to the panel's scope, indicating that generative AI tools are now used directly in World Bank analytical output.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A small but concrete data point on AI penetration into multilateral institutions' research workflow.
insights.quote: Claude-generated graph using the AEA registry based on keywords related to the GAPS scope

themes.theme: GAPS design and the Smart Buys precedent

insights.claim: The Center for Global Development and the World Bank Group are launching the Global Advisory Panel on Skills, which over two years will conduct a systematic review of empirical evidence and produce actionable recommendations on which skills interventions deliver the greatest returns in income, in which contexts, for whom, and at what scale.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A named two-year process whose output will steer donor and government skills budgets, so its scope decisions are worth tracking early.
insights.locator: CGD and the World Bank Group are teaming up

insights.claim: GAPS follows the model of the Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel, which pioneered the "Smart Buys" list that policymakers around the world now use to guide education spending, and aims to build the equivalent ranking for skills.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The Smart Buys precedent shows this format actually redirects national spending, so a skills equivalent will create winners and losers among intervention categories and their providers.
insights.locator: So how will GAPS actually do this?

insights.claim: GAPS starts with four scope areas: training for people already in work including upskilling, reskilling, entrepreneurship courses and farmer field schools; formal routes into work including TVET, apprenticeships and school-to-work programs; ways for workers to prove skills through certification and signaling credentialing; and programs bundling training with broader labor market support such as poverty graduation, cash plus and job matching.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: These four buckets define which intervention types are eligible to be ranked as high-return, effectively setting the competitive field for skills funding.
insights.locator: GAPS will start with four key areas

insights.claim: GAPS deliberately takes a broader scope than prior mapping efforts such as 3ie's evidence gap map on technical and vocational education and training, and will cover informal work, agriculture and self-employment where most people in low- and middle-income countries actually make their living.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Extending the evidence base to informal and self-employed work is where the population actually is, and where formal-sector training evidence has been least applicable.
insights.locator: While others have carried out mapping and synthesis efforts

insights.claim: Two bodies will run GAPS: an intentionally diverse Expert Panel of academics and technical practitioners drawn from low-, middle- and high-income countries that defines scope and distills evidence with cost and scale in mind, and a Steering Committee of implementing organizations, private-sector representatives, policymakers and bilateral and multilateral organizations that leads outreach and translation into action.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Private-sector representation on the steering body means employers will help shape which skills interventions get certified as high-return.
insights.locator: Two groups will drive the GAPS work

insights.claim: Over the next 18 months GAPS will deliver action-focused recommendations on cost-effective, scalable skills interventions, sharing early insights through blog posts and structured dialogue before a short final report launches a wider global conversation.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Gives a dated timeline for when the recommendations become public and start moving budgets.
insights.locator: What's next and how can you follow along?

insights.claim: The initiative is part of the Center for Global Development's collaboration with the Smart Buys Alliance and contributes to the World Bank Group's effort to put skills and jobs at the heart of its business.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Confirms a strategic reorientation of World Bank programming toward jobs and skills, which shapes future lending composition.
insights.locator: This evidence initiative is part of CGD's collaboration
